It is an instance of works_793.json jetty: 600 d, 90 days to make, 30 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Excavations at Wijk bij Duurstede, Hoogstraat (van Es and Verwers) (?)

unlocks.name: A house for the poor at Dorestad
unlocks.what_it_is: Dorestad had many churches, priests and clerics, and 'a multitude of poor people'. Catla of Birka came there with her dead mother's alms and gave them out with the advice of devout women. A house by the upper church where the poor and strangers are fed is what such alms became when a rich man made them lasting.

how_won.plain: Promised before the priest of the upper church and paid for; or given finished by a chain.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = dorestad and standing >= known

unlocks.what_it_gives: The poor of the bank know your boat: word from the river mouth reaches you a day sooner. Your name is said at mass there, and there is a grave for you by the church. It is an instance of works_793.json hospice: 900 d, 120 days to make, 80 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 20 (Robinson 1921); reputation_793.json gave_alms

unlocks.name: A bell for the church at Sliesthorp
unlocks.what_it_is: The younger King Horik let the Christians of Sliesthorp have a bell in their church, 'the use of which the pagans regarded as unlawful'. Somebody paid for the bronze.

how_won.plain: From about 854, with the king's man's leave. Copper and tin brought to the founder come off the price.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = sliesthorp and year >= 854

unlocks.what_it_gives: Christian merchants trust the port and you. The men of the old faith there think less of it. Heard on the water in fog, it makes the last reach of the Slie one word safer for every ship. It is an instance of works_793.json bell: 480 d, 60 days to make, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 32 (Robinson 1921); the bell found in Hedeby harbour is of about 950 (?)

unlocks.name: The church at Birka made new
unlocks.what_it_is: Herigar, the prefect of Birka, built a church on his own land after Ansgar's first visit. About 845 the heathen rose, killed a priest and drove the bishop out, and for seven years there was no priest. When Ansgar came back about 852 the king gave ground for a church again.

how_won.plain: From about 852: timber and silver for the new church, with the prefect's leave.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = birka and year >= 852 and tongue.old_norse >= 0.5

unlocks.what_it_gives: The Christians of Birka count you as the church's founder with the prefect. A priest who can write a letter is found for you whenever one is in the town. It is an instance of works_793.json church_rebuilt: 1800 d, 240 days to make, 40 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 11, 17 and 28 (Robinson 1921), chapter numbers from memory (?); chronicle_793.json 829-ansgar-birka

unlocks.name: The church at Ripa
unlocks.what_it_is: The younger King Horik gave ground at Ripa for a church and let a priest live there. It was the second church in the Danes' land.

how_won.plain: From about 855: silver or timber for the building, with the king's man's leave.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = ripa and year >= 855

unlocks.what_it_gives: The king's man counts you among those the king has given leave to. A grave there for a Christian of the house. It is an instance of works_793.json church_rebuilt: 1800 d, 240 days to make, 40 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 32 (Robinson 1921). The catalogue's kind is for a burned church made new; this one was new: the rules are the same

unlocks.name: A mooring at Æthelred's hythe
unlocks.what_it_is: When London was restored inside its walls, the river bank at Æthelred's hythe was shared out in plots, each with the right to moor ships along its own width and to trade there.

how_won.plain: From 889: a plot-holder's share of the piling and the hard.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = lundenwic and year >= 889 and flag.unlock_plot_lundenwic

unlocks.what_it_gives: Your ships lie at your own frontage and are not moved for anyone. Goods sold on the frontage pay the lord of the plot, not the king's reeve: half toll there for good. It is an instance of works_793.json jetty: 600 d, 90 days to make, 30 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: Sawyer S 346 (889) and S 1628 (898 or 899): works_793.json plot gives them as verified

unlocks.name: A bridge for a soul
unlocks.what_it_is: In the lands of the Svear, once they were Christian, people built bridges and causeways over wet ground for the souls of their dead and said so on a stone. Jarlabanki 'had these stones raised in memory of himself while alive, and made this bridge for his soul'.

how_won.plain: From about 1000: pay for the bridge on the road to the landing, and for the stone beside it.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = uppsalir and year >= 1000

unlocks.what_it_gives: Carters reach the landing in wet weather: the market there is better stocked in spring and autumn. Your dead are named on the stone beside it (a memorial of kind rune stone at no further cost). It is an instance of works_793.json bridge_share: 600 d, 60 days to make, 20 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: the Jarlabanki stones at Täby, c. 1050 (U 127, U 164, U 212, U 261), wording from memory (?); runes_793.json dynna_n68

unlocks.name: The emperor's own merchant
unlocks.what_it_is: Louis the Pious gave certain merchants a letter in 828: they are under his protection, nobody may seize their ships as if for the king's service, they pay no toll anywhere in the realm except the tenth at Quentovic, at Dorestad and at the Alpine passes, and their lawsuits wait for the emperor or the master he has set over the merchants. In return they come to the palace in the middle of May, every year or every second year, and serve the emperor's chamber faithfully from their trade.

how_won.plain: An audience at the palace with a count or bishop to speak for you, a gift to the chamber, and a house the delta trusts.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year >= 814 and year <= 840 and standing_region >= trusted and silver >= 240

unlocks.what_it_gives: Counts as unlock_charter_<port> at every port of realm franks except dorestad and quentovic, where the tenth is still paid. A seizure by the king's men ('law seizure') is turned into a hearing you are 'likely' to win. Duty: be at Noviomagus in May at least every second year with a gift of 60 d or its worth; miss it twice and the flag is cleared.
unlocks.source: Formulae imperiales no. 37, Praeceptum negotiatorum (828), MGH Formulae ed. Zeumer: from memory, wording not checked (?)

unlocks.name: A seat among the merchants of Tiel
unlocks.what_it_is: Alpert of Metz, writing about 1021 to 1024, did not like the merchants of Tiel. They judge by their own will and not by the law, and say the emperor gave them that right by charter. A man may clear himself of a debt by his own oath. They keep a common purse, and on set days of the year they drink together from early morning. They swear and drink together.

how_won.plain: Trade in the Waal and the Rhine mouth three years, be trusted in the delta, pay the entry and swear the brothers' oath at a feast.
how_won.when: moored and year >= 1000 and standing_region >= trusted and silver >= 240 and (port.id = traiectum or port.id = daventre or port.id = noviomagus)

unlocks.what_it_gives: Among the brothers a claim of debt against you is ended by your own oath (no 'law' case, no lost_case). The seat itself is works_793.json guild_seat (240 d, and 24 d each winter to the common purse; after a wreck the chest lends up to 300 d with no day set; a dead brother is buried at the brothers' cost). Brothers tell each other prices: word from Tiel's trade in England and on the Rhine is a week fresher. In London you are one of the emperor's men (unlock_title_emperors_man). The bishop's people like you less.
unlocks.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20 (chronicle_793.json 1020-tiel-merchants, 1018-07-29-vlaardingen); TIEL HAS NO ROW IN ports_793.json: until it has, the seat is offered at Traiectum, Daventre or Noviomagus

unlocks.name: A thegn's right
unlocks.what_it_is: An English text of Archbishop Wulfstan's time (1002 to 1023) remembers how it once was: a merchant who throve so that he crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost was from then on worthy of a thegn's right. A thegn's oath outweighs a common man's, his life is priced at six times as much, and he stands near the king's business.

how_won.plain: Cross the open sea to or from an English port three times in a ship of your own, with your own cargo, and be well regarded in an English realm. It is the game's own three-crossings rule: say so when it happens.
how_won.when: moored and standing_region >= well_regarded and (port.realm = wessex or port.realm = mercia or port.realm = kent or port.realm = eastanglia or port.realm = northumbria)

unlocks.what_it_gives: In English realms: your standing cannot fall below known; your oath wins a lawsuit as 'likely' where it was 'doubtful'; the reeve seats you at his court (act:hear_law and act:witness are open). Duties: from 1008 a share in the king's ship-levy (60 d in a levy year), and on your death the heir pays a heriot before he takes the house (120 d: a horse and its gear, or its worth).
unlocks.source: Geþyncðo ('Of people's ranks and law'), the merchant clause of the Textus Roffensis text (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geþyncðo, read 4 Oct 2026); Thorpe 1840 gives it as: 'if a merchant thrived, so that he fared thrice over the wide sea by his own means, then was he thenceforth of thane-right worthy' (wording from memory: check before it is shown) (?); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1008; II Cnut 71 for the heriot (?). The heir keeps the right only while the house still has a ship of its own

unlocks.name: A brother of the Frisians' guild at Sigtuna
unlocks.what_it_is: Two rune stones at Sigtuna were raised by 'the Frisians' guild-brothers' for dead brothers: one for Thorkel, one for Albod, who was the partner of a man named Slodi. They ask God to help the soul. By then 'Frisian' may have meant any merchant of the western trade.

how_won.plain: From about 1050: a house of Frisian name that has traded three summers in the lake of the Svear is asked to the guild's drinking.
how_won.when: moored and year >= 1050 and tongue.old_norse >= 0.5 and standing >= well_regarded and port.id = uppsalir

unlocks.what_it_gives: The brothers stand surety for you among the Svear; a brother who dies abroad is given a stone with his name (a memorial of kind rune stone, paid by the guild). 24 d each winter to the guild's purse.
unlocks.source: runes_793.json sigtuna_u379 (U 379); U 391 for Albod; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrkogården_Runestones, read 4 Oct 2026. SIGTUNA HAS NO ROW IN ports_793.json: uppsalir stands in, as in runes_793.json

unlocks.name: One of the emperor's men at London
unlocks.what_it_is: London's toll rules of about 1000 say that the men of the emperor who came in their ships were held worthy of good laws, like the Londoners themselves. They paid in kind at Christmas and at Easter: cloth, pepper, gloves and vinegar.

how_won.plain: From about 1000: a house whose home is in the emperor's lands (the Rhine and the delta) and that is known at Lundenwic.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = lundenwic and year >= 1000 and standing >= known

unlocks.what_it_gives: At Lundenwic you trade as a Londoner does: no toll on each sale, but a fixed render twice a year (at Christmas and at Easter: 3 wool_cloth, 2 pepper and 10 d, or the toll is taken as before). You may buy wool and provisions for your own ship without the reeve's leave.
unlocks.source: IV Æthelred 2 (chronicle_793.json 1000-london-tolls); the items of the render are from memory (grey and brown cloth, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves, two casks of vinegar) (?)

unlocks.name: A lord's protection
unlocks.what_it_is: A free man could put himself under the hand of a count, a bishop or an abbot: the lord speaks for him in court and against other lords' men, and he serves the lord in what a free man may. The emperor's letters of protection for named merchants survive.

how_won.plain: An audience with a lord who is at least friendly with you, a gift, and an oath to do his errands.
how_won.when: moored and port.realm = franks and port.best_feeling >= friendly and silver >= 60

unlocks.what_it_gives: In that lord's district: the king's men search you less (the search weight halved), a case against you is heard by the lord himself ('likely' in your favour), and the debt's day can be put off once by a season. Duty: one errand a year carried for him with no premium (a commission at premium 0). His enemies are yours.
unlocks.source: Formulae Turonenses 43 (a formula of commendation, 8th century) (?); Formulae imperiales 30, 31, 37, 52 (letters of protection for merchants) (?)

unlocks.name: A moneyer's die
unlocks.what_it_is: English pennies carry the name of the man who struck them: Eoba and Ibba for Offa, and so on down to 1066. King Æthelstan's law names how many moneyers each town has, and says a moneyer found false loses the hand he did it with, which is then set up over his workshop.

how_won.plain: A rich townsman known to the reeve, with a house in a town that has a mint, buys the office when a moneyer dies.
how_won.when: moored and port.has_mint > 0 and standing >= trusted and silver >= 600 and (port.realm = wessex or port.realm = mercia or port.realm = kent or port.realm = eastanglia or port.realm = northumbria)

unlocks.what_it_gives: At that mint: act:change_coin costs you nothing, and the office pays 80 d at each winter reckoning. Your name is on the coin: standing in that realm rises slowly without your doing anything. The dishonest road is open (strike light pennies: 200 d more a year, and each year a 'doubtful' chance of being found out, which costs the hand, the office and the standing of the house).
unlocks.source: npc_roles_793.json moneyer; II Æthelstan (Grately) 14 (chronicle_793.json 928-grately-laws); price a guess (?)

unlocks.name: The king's guest
unlocks.what_it_is: Ohthere, a Northman who traded and took tribute in the far north, told his voyages to 'his lord, King Alfred', and brought him walrus teeth. A king wants to hear of seas he has not seen, and he names the man who tells him.

how_won.plain: Bring a king what his hall lacks (three kept commissions at a royal seat), be trusted there, and tell him of a voyage: a voyage text in the chest, or a far port he has only heard of.
how_won.when: moored and standing >= trusted and port.best_feeling >= fast_friend and (port.id = hamwic or port.id = bebbanburg or port.id = hleidr or port.id = uppsalir or port.id = ogvaldsnes or port.id = noviomagus)

unlocks.what_it_gives: An audience whenever the king is at that seat. A gift from him at each Yule or Easter you are there (60 to 120 d, or a ring). Raiders who are that king's men let you pass. Other kings' men look at you twice.
unlocks.source: texts_793.json ohthere (Bosworth 1859); riddles_793.json rw_favour_uppsalir, rw_favour_hleidr

unlocks.name: A cloth from Boniface's church at Doccinga
unlocks.what_it_is: Boniface was killed by the Dokkum river on 5 June 754. His body went to Fulda. On the place a mound was raised against the tides and a church built on it, and a spring of sweet water rose there. A strip of cloth that has lain on the altar of the place is a relic an honest priest can give.

how_won.plain: Go to Doccinga on the saint's day or to keep a vow (flag vow_doccinga, from the winter card harbour.winter.vow) and give alms there.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = doccinga and (flag.vow_doccinga or month = 6) and silver >= 24

unlocks.what_it_gives: A relic of the first class a merchant can honestly hold. Frisian and Frankish hands take heart from it. See relic_uses for what can be done with it.
unlocks.source: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii c. 8-9 (the mound, the church and the spring); Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri (Liudger served the church at Dokkum) (?)

unlocks.name: A cloth from Cuthbert's coffin
unlocks.what_it_is: Cuthbert's body lay whole in its carved oak coffin at Lindisfarne from 698. After the heathen came in 793 the monks stayed; in 875 they took the coffin and wandered seven years with it. A cloth laid on the coffin was given to those who helped the house.

how_won.plain: Help the monks: bring what they are short of after the raid (three kept commissions at Lindisfarena) or carry their letters south.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = lindisfarena and year < 875 and standing >= well_regarded

unlocks.what_it_gives: English hands take heart from it; Northumbrians trust the man who carries it (standing in Northumbria one step quicker to rise). See relic_uses for what can be done with it.
unlocks.source: Anonymous and Bede's Lives of Cuthbert; Symeon of Durham for the wandering of 875-883 (?); chronicle_793.json for 793

unlocks.name: A bone of a Roman martyr
unlocks.what_it_is: From 827 Roman bones came north in number. Einhard's notary took Marcellinus and Peter out of their tomb by night with the help of a Roman deacon named Deusdona, who went on supplying the abbeys of the Rhine for years. The bones were real. The names were sometimes hopeful.

how_won.plain: Bought at a Rhine town from a man with a Roman way of talking, or at your own door in winter (the winter card harbour.winter.relic_hawker).
how_won.when: moored and year >= 827 and silver >= 60 and (port.id = mogontia or port.id = colonia or port.id = traiectum)

unlocks.what_it_gives: A relic of uncertain name until a bishop proves it. If proven, the best gift a merchant can make a new church. See relic_uses for what can be done with it.
unlocks.source: Einhard, Translatio et miracula sanctorum Marcellini et Petri (827-830); Rudolf of Fulda on Deusdona's later journeys (?); winter_793.json harbour.winter.relic_hawker

unlocks.name: A bone that is nobody's
unlocks.what_it_is: Charlemagne's great capitulary of 789 warns against false names of martyrs and against wanderers who go about deceiving people. There was a market for them, or there would have been no warning.

how_won.plain: You were sold it (the bad branch of harbour.winter.relic_hawker), or you made it.

unlocks.what_it_gives: It does nothing a relic does. It can be sold on (dishonest: see relic_uses 'Sell a false one') or burned. While the flag is set, any bishop who is asked to prove a relic of yours looks at all of them. A LASTING COST, not a reward.
unlocks.source: Admonitio generalis 789 c. 42 and c. 79

unlocks.name: The folding scales and their weights
unlocks.what_it_is: A small bronze balance that folds into a tinned box, with a set of weights: the tool of every man who takes silver by weight. They lie in merchants' graves at Birka and Hedeby and in the earth at Dorestad. From about 870 the weights of the east are little iron balls with flattened poles, cased in bronze so nobody can file them.

how_won.plain: Bought from a smith or a goldsmith (town_actions_793.json act:buy_tools, the second purchase: flag act_own_scales), and then kept: when the house has had its own balance through three winters, or a dead partner leaves his, it is an heirloom.

unlocks.what_it_gives: While it is aboard it is the town act's balance (act:weigh_silver and act:test_silver cost no fee and cannot be cheated). As an heirloom it is never lost with a boat, and an heir who has his father's scales is taken for his father's son: one person at each port where the father weighed silver keeps his feeling whole at the succession.
unlocks.source: town_actions_793.json buy_tools, weigh_silver; npc_roles_793.json goldsmith; balances and weights from the Birka graves and Hedeby; the standard oblate weights from about 870 (?)

unlocks.name: A sword with a name in the blade
unlocks.what_it_is: Rhineland smiths welded a maker's name in iron letters into the blade: +VLFBERH+T is on more than a hundred swords found from Ireland to the Volga. The emperor's laws of 803, 805 and 811 forbid selling such blades out of the realm, which is why they are found there.

how_won.plain: A lord's gift for a great service, or bought at Colonia by a man the smith trusts, never for carrying north.
how_won.when: moored and port.id = colonia and standing >= trusted and silver >= 480

unlocks.what_it_gives: It hangs in the house and goes to the heir. Worn at an audience it makes a merchant look like a man who has a lord (one step better with counts and chiefs). Carried out of the realm it is a forbidden good: 'hold.weapons' counts it.
unlocks.source: npc_roles_793.json smith, kings_man; chronicle_793.json 803-arms-to-merchants-803, 805-12-thionville-arms, 811-10-boulogne-capitulary, 864-06-25-pitres; price a guess (?)

unlocks.name: A gilded weather vane
unlocks.what_it_is: In the eleventh century a great ship carried a vane of gilded bronze at her stem or masthead, cut with a beast and hung with rattling tags: four survive, later nailed to church spires in Sweden and Norway.

how_won.plain: From about 1000: a king's or a chief's gift to a shipowner, or ordered from a goldsmith by a house of rank.
how_won.when: moored and year >= 1000 and standing >= trusted and silver >= 360

unlocks.what_it_gives: On your own ship it is seen two miles off: every port knows who is coming before she moors (your standing counts at first sight; raiders who fear your lord sheer off, and raiders who do not come closer).
unlocks.source: the vanes of Källunge, Söderala, Heggen and Tingelstad, 11th century (?)

unlocks.name: A long knife with the rune row
unlocks.what_it_is: A single-edged knife found in the Thames has the whole English rune row inlaid along its blade in silver and copper wire, and a name after it: Beagnoth.

how_won.plain: Made by an English smith for a man who can tell him the runes, or won at a riddling.
how_won.when: moored and port.realm != franks and learned.runes >= 0.5 and silver >= 120

unlocks.what_it_gives: The house's own rune row to learn from: an heir who has it starts with learned.runes 0.5. An Englishman or a Northman who sees it reckons you can read.
unlocks.source: the Thames seax of Beagnoth, British Museum, 9th or 10th century (?)

unlocks.name: A drinking horn bound in silver
unlocks.what_it_is: The horn of a great ox with a silver rim and tip, passed from hand to hand at a feast. In the English riddle the horn says it was once a fighter's weapon and now a maiden fills it.

how_won.plain: A lord's gift at a feast, or bought from a goldsmith.

unlocks.what_it_gives: A feast held with it (act:feast, the winter's Yule card) lifts the crew's heart one tenth more. It is what a guest remembers of your house.
unlocks.source: texts_793.json exeter_14_horn; price a guess (?)

unlocks.name: A silver arm-ring of full weight
unlocks.what_it_is: In the north a man's silver is on his arm: rings made to a known weight, cut up when change is needed. A ring given by a lord is kept whole and shown.

how_won.plain: A chief's or a king's gift for a service, or a partner's parting gift.
how_won.when: moored and tongue.old_norse >= 0.5 and port.best_feeling >= fast_friend

unlocks.what_it_gives: Worth 100 d by weight if it must be cut (the last reserve of the house: it can pay a ransom or a debt's last part). Kept whole, it is proof of whose man you are: that lord's people know it on sight.
unlocks.source: riddles_793.json rw_hoard_huxley (flattened silver arm-rings); arm-rings in every northern hoard

unlocks.name: A black jug with tin leaves
unlocks.what_it_is: A fine dark jug from the Rhineland, dressed with patterns cut from tin foil. They are found at Dorestad, in graves at Birka, at Hedeby and in English ports: a thing for wine at a good table or at the altar.

how_won.plain: Bought at Dorestad or Colonia while they are still made.

unlocks.what_it_gives: One unit of tating_ware kept out of the hold for the house. A guest of rank served from it thinks better of you (gifts at act:feast count one step more).
unlocks.source: goods_793.json tating_ware; Tating ware, c. 770-830 (?)

unlocks.name: A hammer and a cross on one cord
unlocks.what_it_is: A soapstone mould found in Jutland cast Thor's hammers and Christ's crosses side by side: the smith sold whichever the customer wanted, and some wanted both.

how_won.plain: Given by a Norse partner or crewman after a hard crossing, or bought from a smith in a Danish port from about 900.
how_won.when: moored and year >= 900 and (port.realm = danes or port.realm = norse_vestfold or port.realm = svear)

unlocks.what_it_gives: Worn under the shirt. Men of either faith aboard take it as their own sign: the heart of a mixed crew does not fall for quarrels of faith. A bishop who sees it does not laugh.
unlocks.source: the Trendgården mould, National Museum of Denmark, 10th century; BRIEF.md tone guide

unlocks.name: A Frisian wife
unlocks.what_it_is: Marriage was a bargain between two kins, made before witnesses: the man gives the bride-gift, names what she will have if she outlives him, and gives her a morning-gift after the first night. Among the Frisians, who takes a free woman without the will of those who have power over her pays her guardian twenty shillings.

how_won.plain: The chain house_marriage (a farmer's daughter of Winaldum); or, for a later head of the house, the winter card harbour.winter.wedding (a neighbour's daughter).
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and not flag.house_wed and silver >= 60

unlocks.what_it_gives: Her brothers and uncles on the Frisian shore are yours: a second boat in the family is easier to come by (the cost of unlock_partner_kinsman halved). Sets the house's flag house_wed too when it comes from the winter card. The house has a mistress who runs the plot, the loom and the store while the boat is away: the winter cards for a child, for weaving and for a vow open. Her kin are your oath-helpers in a lawsuit (one word better). The four unlock_kin_wife_ flags say of which people she is; the chain house_marriage gives each with far more than this (Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md). A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Lex Frisionum IX.11 (as read in Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md); the Old English tract 'Be wifmannes beweddunge' (c. 1000) for the form of a betrothal (?); winter_793.json harbour.winter.wedding

unlocks.name: An English wife
unlocks.what_it_is: Frisians lived at York before 793 and traded in every English port. An English wife brings her tongue, her father's roof in his port, and his word for you among his people. In Kent a maiden was 'bought with cattle', and the morning-gift was hers.

how_won.plain: The chain house_marriage (the kin at Eoforwic); or the winter card harbour.winter.wedding, for a house that already has a plot, a factor or a guest-friend in an English port.
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and not flag.house_wed and silver >= 120 and (flag.unlock_plot_lundenwic or flag.unlock_plot_eoforwic or flag.unlock_factor_lundenwic or flag.unlock_factor_eoforwic or flag.guest_friend_eoforwic)

unlocks.what_it_gives: Sets house_wife_foreign from the winter card. English is spoken in the house: the merchant has it in full after two winters and the heir from birth. At her father's port: lodging free, standing never below known, and her father a friend from the start. Sets the house's flag house_wed too when it comes from the winter card. The house has a mistress who runs the plot, the loom and the store while the boat is away: the winter cards for a child, for weaving and for a vow open. Her kin are your oath-helpers in a lawsuit (one word better). The four unlock_kin_wife_ flags say of which people she is; the chain house_marriage gives each with far more than this (Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md). A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Laws of Æthelberht 77 and 81 (as read in Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md); Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 for the Frisians of York (?); winter_793.json harbour.winter.wedding

unlocks.name: A Frankish wife
unlocks.what_it_is: The daughter of a bishop's or a count's steward: a house with letters in it, and a dower set down in a written deed before the priest, who must first ask into the degrees of kinship between the two.

how_won.plain: The chain house_marriage (the bishop's steward's daughter at Traiectum).

unlocks.what_it_gives: She reads, and the house begins to (Latin letters come more easily: each winter's learning counts half as much again). Her father's lord is the house's road to a charter or a plot. Sets the house's flag house_wed too when it comes from the winter card. The house has a mistress who runs the plot, the loom and the store while the boat is away: the winter cards for a child, for weaving and for a vow open. Her kin are your oath-helpers in a lawsuit (one word better). The four unlock_kin_wife_ flags say of which people she is; the chain house_marriage gives each with far more than this (Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md). A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Capitulary of 802 c. 35 (as read in Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md)

unlocks.name: A Danish wife
unlocks.what_it_is: The daughter of the Dane who answers for Frisian ships at Ripa: a marriage made by a handclasp and silver on the scale, between two faiths. Whether her gods come with her is the question the priest at home will ask.

how_won.plain: The chain house_marriage (the host's daughter at Ripa).

unlocks.what_it_gives: The Danes' tongue is spoken in the house: the merchant has it in full and the heir from birth. Among the Danes of her father's coast the house is not a stranger. Sets the house's flag house_wed too when it comes from the winter card. The house has a mistress who runs the plot, the loom and the store while the boat is away: the winter cards for a child, for weaving and for a vow open. Her kin are your oath-helpers in a lawsuit (one word better). The four unlock_kin_wife_ flags say of which people she is; the chain house_marriage gives each with far more than this (Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md). A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md; npc_roles_793.json host

unlocks.name: A sister married into a rival house
unlocks.what_it_is: A woman given in marriage between two houses that have quarrelled was called a peace-weaver by the English poets. Sometimes it held.

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.sister_offer.
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and not flag.house_sister_wed and standing >= known

unlocks.what_it_gives: That house stops undercutting you: it is no longer one of the named rivals at your home port, and its skippers share word with yours. If she is treated badly, the feud is worse than before (flag house_feud_rival). A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Beowulf (the peace-weaver: texts_793.json beowulf_28 and beowulf_29, Hall 1892); research_scale_to_fleets.md 7.5 (rivals as named houses)

unlocks.name: A lord's man stood sponsor to your child
unlocks.what_it_is: The one who lifts a child from the font is kin to its parents from that day: kin in God, which the Church counted as near as blood. Kings used it: Louis the Pious stood sponsor to the Dane Harald in 826, Alfred to Guthrum in 878.

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.godparent, for a house the port knows.
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and flag.house_child and standing >= known and silver >= 24

unlocks.what_it_gives: The count's man speaks for the house when the debt's day comes (one delay of a season, once), and his lord's court is 'likely' yours. A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: Annales regni Francorum 826; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 878; winter_793.json harbour.winter.godparent

unlocks.name: A fellow merchant stood sponsor to your child
unlocks.what_it_is: Kin in God with a man of your own trade: his house and yours eat together at feasts and stand surety for each other.

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.godparent.

unlocks.what_it_gives: He will be a partner if asked (the cost of unlock_partner_neighbour halved), and takes in the household if your house burns or floods. A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: as above; winter_793.json harbour.winter.godparent

unlocks.name: A son fostered in the north
unlocks.what_it_is: Among the Northmen a child was often brought up in another man's house, and the tie was as strong as birth. A cross on Man says it in runes: 'Better to leave a good foster-son than a bad son.'

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.foster, for a man who has the Norse tongue in part.
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and flag.house_child and tongue.old_norse >= 0.5

unlocks.what_it_gives: Sets flag house_heir_norse: the heir has the Norse tongue in full, knows runes in part, and has a foster-father's hall in a Danish or Norse port (lodging, surety, a friend who is a fast friend from the start). He comes home with a Dane's opinions. A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: runes_793.json manx_michael104 (Kermode 1907); fostering is described in the sagas, written down later

unlocks.name: A Dane's son in your house
unlocks.what_it_is: The other half of the same custom: he who fosters another man's child does him honour and binds him.

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.foster.

unlocks.what_it_gives: The Norse tongue is spoken at your own table: the merchant has it in full ('tongue old_norse = 1'). The boy's father is your friend in his port and answers for you there. If the house has no child, the foster-son can be named heir. A tie of kin outlives the man who made it: the heir keeps it, with the other house's feeling halved like every feeling at a succession.
unlocks.source: as above; winter_793.json harbour.winter.foster

unlocks.name: A son given to the church
unlocks.what_it_is: Parents gave a child to a monastery with a gift, his hand wrapped in the altar cloth. He could not come back. He learned letters, and a house with a monk in it has a scribe, a reader of charters and a voice near an abbot.

how_won.plain: The winter card harbour.winter.school, the second choice.
how_won.when: moored and flag.wintering and flag.house_child and silver >= 40

unlocks.what_it_gives: The house loses that child as an heir. It gains: letters read and written without fee wherever he is; that monastery's commissions offered to you first; a 'likely' welcome from its abbot. deed gave_alms.
unlocks.source: Rule of St Benedict c. 59 (the offering of children); npc_roles_793.json child; winter_793.json harbour.winter.school

unlocks.name: A kinsman bought back
unlocks.what_it_is: Raiders sold whom they took. Buying a Christian back was among the best of good works: Ansgar bought boys from the Danes and the Wends, and a Frisian in London once let a captured Northumbrian thegn go to find his own ransom.

how_won.plain: Find him: word of where he was sold comes by ship, late. Then pay the dealer's price or carry what the dealer wants.
how_won.when: moored and silver >= 240 and (port.id = sliesthorp or port.id = ripa or port.id = birka or port.id = duiblinn or port.id = rotomagus)

unlocks.what_it_gives: A grown kinsman who owes the house his life: a skipper who does not leave (he can take unlock_partner_kinsman at no cost) and who knows the port where he was held, its tongue in part and its dealers by name. deed bought_captives counts for you here, not against.
unlocks.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 15 and 35 (Robinson 1921) (?); Bede, Historia ecclesiastica IV.22 (Imma and the Frisian of London); npc_roles_793.json slave_dealer, captive; price a guess (?)

unlocks.name: English
unlocks.what_it_is: The speech of all the English kingdoms. It is so near Frisian that a Frisian has half of it from birth: the missionaries who went to Frisia from England preached without an interpreter (?).

how_won.plain: Half (0.5): a hand of that people aboard for one sailing season, or a winter guest (winter_793.json). Full (1): a winter spent in that land, a wife or a foster-son of that people, or a factor's house there for two years. A Frisian starts at 0.5.

unlocks.what_it_gives: The house's own tongue is Old Frisian. A tongue is had aboard at 0, 0.5 or 1 (npc_text_encounters.md 2.6): at 0.5 nouns and numbers are understood, at 1 everything. Set with the effect 'tongue <name> = f'. With it: lines in that tongue are read in full, prices are a little better where it is the market's tongue, and its people give one more piece of news a call. An heir has it only if it was spoken in the house (a foreign wife, a foster-son) or he sailed two seasons with it aboard.
unlocks.source: npc_text_encounters.md 2.6 (kin table); npc_roles_793.json peoples

The hand to hire for it is a Dane.

unlocks.what_it_is: What is spoken at Truso and Grobina. Wulfstan, who sailed there, says the Este have many towns and a king in each.

how_won.plain: Half (0.5): a hand of that people aboard for one sailing season, or a winter guest (winter_793.json). Full (1): a winter spent in that land, a wife or a foster-son of that people, or a factor's house there for two years. Starts at 0.

unlocks.what_it_is: Spoken by the fur-hunters of the north and around Ladoga. Ohthere says the Finnas and the Beormas seemed to him to speak nearly one language.

how_won.plain: Half (0.5): a hand of that people aboard for one sailing season, or a winter guest (winter_793.json). Full (1): a winter spent in that land, a wife or a foster-son of that people, or a factor's house there for two years. Starts at 0. A Rus trader at Aldeigjuborg is the usual go-between.

unlocks.name: Irish
unlocks.what_it_is: The speech of Ireland and of the Scots of Dalriata, with the oldest written learning in the north after Latin.

how_won.plain: Half (0.5): a hand of that people aboard for one sailing season, or a winter guest (winter_793.json). Full (1): a winter spent in that land, a wife or a foster-son of that people, or a factor's house there for two years. Starts at 0. An Irish monk abroad teaches it gladly, with Latin.

unlocks.what_it_gives: The house's own tongue is Old Frisian. A tongue is had aboard at 0, 0.5 or 1 (npc_text_encounters.md 2.6): at 0.5 nouns and numbers are understood, at 1 everything. unlocks.name: Latin letters
unlocks.what_it_is: The Roman alphabet and enough Latin to read a charter, a letter or a schoolbook riddle. In 789 the king ordered schools for boys in every monastery and bishop's house. A layman who could read was rare, and useful.

how_won.plain: A monk carried as a passenger for forty days; a winter guest who teaches (harbour.winter.monk_guest: half each winter); a winter spent at a monastery; or an heir sent to school (harbour.winter.school).

unlocks.what_it_gives: The condition variable learned.latin (0 to 1; the chest reads Latin when it is 1, or when a reader is aboard). With it: every Latin text in the chest is read; a charter is read before it is trusted, so a false one cannot be sold to you; letters to a factor need no hired scribe; clerks and bishops deal one step more easily with you. An heir has it only if he was schooled (flag house_heir_lettered).
unlocks.source: Admonitio generalis 789 c. 72 (schools); npc_text_encounters.md 2.6; npc_roles_793.json schoolmaster, scribe, monk

unlocks.name: Runes: the short row of the north
unlocks.what_it_is: Sixteen runes, cut with a knife across the grain of a stick: by about 800 the Danes and Northmen had cut the old row of twenty-four down to this. Sticks with messages, names and verses lie in the mud of Hedeby's harbour. Anyone who trades in the north needs to read an owner's mark and a tally.

how_won.plain: A Norse hand or winter guest cuts the row for you and you copy it (harbour.winter.norse_guest: half each winter); a rune-carver at a Danish or Svear port teaches it for silver.

unlocks.what_it_gives: The condition variable learned.runes (0 to 1). With it: rune sticks in the chest are read; you can cut your own price sticks and messages (a reply to a partner needs no go-between); you read the stones by the road, some of which say where a man died and what he owned. An heir has it if he was fostered in the north or was left the runed knife.
unlocks.source: runes_793.json futhark and inscriptions; npc_roles_793.json rune_carver

unlocks.name: Runes: the English and Frisian row
unlocks.what_it_is: The older, longer row as the English and the Frisians kept and added to it, twenty-eight runes and more. It is on Cuthbert's coffin, on the Northumbrian crosses, on English and Frisian pennies and on a yew stick from a Frisian mound. By 793 the Church writes Latin letters and the runes are for names, marks and memorials.

how_won.plain: An old Frisian or an English monk who still cuts them shows you; it counts toward the same learning.

unlocks.what_it_gives: Counts as half of learned.runes. With it the runes inside the English riddles are read (texts exeter_19_rider_runes and exeter_24_jay_runes), and the names on English memorial stones.
unlocks.source: npc_roles_793.json rune_carver (Cuthbert's coffin, 698; the Northumbrian crosses); the Westeremden yew stick and the Frisian rune coins (?)

unlocks.name: A grave by the church and a mass each year
unlocks.what_it_is: The Christian dead lie in the churchyard, heads to the west, with nothing in the grave. What marks a merchant is where he lies, how near the wall of the church, and whether a mass is sung for him on the thirtieth day and on the year's day. The marker is wood and does not last.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). Paid to the priest: the soul's gift at the open grave and the masses.
how_won.when: moored and silver >= 30 and (port.realm = franks or port.realm = kent or port.realm = wessex or port.realm = mercia or port.realm = eastanglia or port.realm = northumbria)

unlocks.what_it_gives: The crew's heart rises (they see how the house treats its dead). deed gave_alms. The dead man's kin think well of the house. The chronicle's line for him ends 'and he lies at' with the church's name.
unlocks.source: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 22 (Christians to the church's burial ground, not the mounds of the heathen); soul-scot 'at the open grave' in the later English laws (V Æthelred 12) (?)

formulas.source: the common formula of Christian grave stones in the Rhineland and Gaul
the common request on Christian memorials

unlocks.name: A name in the book of life
unlocks.what_it_is: A monastery kept a book of the names of its brothers, its kings and its friends, living and dead, laid on the altar at mass so that all in it were prayed for together. Lindisfarne's, written about 840 in gold and silver, still exists.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). A gift to the house, large enough to be remembered.
how_won.when: moored and port.kind = monastery and standing >= known

unlocks.what_it_gives: The name is prayed for while the house stands. Standing with that monastery does not decay. An heir who comes there is known by his father's name on the page. It is an instance of works_793.json book_of_life: 240 d, 12 d a year to keep at the winter reckoning, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: the Durham Liber Vitae (Lindisfarne or Wearmouth-Jarrow, c. 840); the confraternity book of Reichenau (c. 824) (?)

formulas.plain: {name}: the name alone, among the others.
formulas.source: a book of life is lists of names under headings such as 'Nomina regum vel ducum' (the Durham Liber Vitae); nothing is said of anyone (?)

unlocks.name: An English stone with a prayer
unlocks.what_it_is: In Northumbria a carved stone was set up 'after' the dead by the one who owed it, in runes or in Roman letters or both, and it asked the passer-by to pray. The stone itself is called a becun, a beacon.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). Cut by an English carver in a Northumbrian port.
how_won.when: moored and port.realm = northumbria and year < 900

unlocks.what_it_gives: The crew's heart rises more than for a grave alone. English men who read it think well of the house. It stands by the road for a thousand years. It is an instance of works_793.json grave_stone: 120 d, 20 days to make, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: the stones of Thornhill and Great Urswick, 8th to 9th century (readings from memory: spelling to be checked) (?); npc_roles_793.json rune_carver

unlocks.name: A stone raised with runes
unlocks.what_it_is: A standing stone by a road, a bridge or a landing, cut and painted: who raised it, for whom, what he was to them, and one thing about him. Few in 793, a fashion from about 970, and thousands by 1066. Partners raised them for partners.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). Cut by a rune-carver for silver; the wording is yours to choose from the formulas.
how_won.when: moored and (port.realm = danes or port.realm = svear or port.realm = gutes or port.realm = norse_vestfold or port.realm = norse_west)

unlocks.what_it_gives: The crew's heart rises. Norse people of that shore know the house keeps faith with its dead: a partner's kin stay the house's friends. The stone can be read by any later traveller of the game (an heir meets it). It is an instance of works_793.json rune_stone: 300 d, 40 days to make, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: runes_793.json (the game's own glosses): hedeby_dr1, helnaes_dr190, mervalla_so198, sigtuna_u379, valleberga_dr337, glavendrup_dr209

formulas.plain: {raiser} raised this stone for {dead}, his partner.

formulas.plain: He was a ship's master, a very good man.

formulas.plain: He often sailed to {place} in a dear ship.

runes_793.json glavendrup_dr209 (DR 209, c. 900-925): the heathen ending

unlocks.name: A Gotland picture stone
unlocks.what_it_is: On Gotland the dead were given a tall stone shaped like a keyhole, carved with pictures and painted: at the foot a ship under full sail with her crew, above it a rider welcomed by a woman with a horn. Some have a line of runes round the edge.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). Only at Paviken, cut by a Gotland stone-carver, for a man who sailed.

unlocks.what_it_gives: As a rune stone, and the Gutes count the house among those who know how things are done. The ship on the stone is cut from yours. It is an instance of works_793.json rune_stone: 300 d, 40 days to make, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: the stones of Tjängvide, Ardre and Lärbro (8th to 10th century) (?); riddles_793.json, a Gotland stone-carver at Paviken

formulas.plain: {raiser} raised the stone after {dead}, his brother.

unlocks.name: A ship of stones
unlocks.what_it_is: Stones set on end in the outline of a ship around a grave, bow and stern stones the tallest. There are hundreds at Lindholm above the Limfjord. At Glavendrup the rune stone itself stands at the prow of one.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). The old faith's way, in a Danish or Svear land: a day's work for the crew and a feast.
how_won.when: moored and crew >= 3 and (port.realm = danes or port.realm = svear or port.realm = norse_vestfold)

unlocks.what_it_gives: Costs a feast and nothing else. Men of the old faith aboard are moved by it more than by any mass (their heart rises twice as much); a priest who hears of it is not.
unlocks.source: the ship settings of Lindholm Høje (c. 700-1000) and Glavendrup (runes_793.json glavendrup_dr209)

unlocks.name: An Irish slab: a prayer for a name
unlocks.what_it_is: The Irish laid a flat stone on the grave, cut with a cross and two words before the name: a prayer for him. The yard at Clonmacnoise is full of them.

how_won.plain: For a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership (act:bury, act:remember, or the winter card harbour.winter.memorial). Cut by a monastery's mason at Hi or Duiblinn.
how_won.when: moored and (port.id = hi or port.id = duiblinn)

unlocks.what_it_gives: As a grave by the church. Irish and Gaelic people who read it think well of the house. It is an instance of works_793.json grave_stone: 120 d, 20 days to make, and that row's 'gives' holds here too.
unlocks.source: the grave slabs of Clonmacnoise, 8th to 11th century (?)

formulas.source: the usual formula of the Clonmacnoise slabs (?)

Written down: c. 1270 (Codex Regius only); Bellows (after Mogk) dates the poem to the 12th c. The words are from a later book; the thing was said in the game's years.

how_won.plain: Given by a farmer of the king's estate (Thor's question, on the same stick as the answer t-alv-32), at Hleiðr (860-1066).

unlocks.what_it_gives: In the chest (text.t-alv-31 is true). Read or heard in full when tongue.old_norse is 1 aboard; in part at 0.5. It is cut in runes: learned.runes at 1 or a hand who reads them.
unlocks.source: texts_793.json t-alv-31: English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (New York, 1923). Old Norse: K. Hildebrand and H. Gering, Die Lieder der älteren Edda (Paderborn, 1904)

needs: Wire every unlock_ flag: the game should read them by prefix (the kinds block) and by the entries' what_it_gives.
harbour.tollman.frankish checks text.charter_toll_dorestad: let 'Show the charter' also open on flag.unlock_charter_<port id>.

A port row for Tiel (from about 896, Zwentibold's toll; burned 1006) and one for Sigtuna (from about 980): unlock_title_tiel_brother and unlock_title_frisian_guild are offered at stand-in ports until then.

Ship classes for the half-decked sea trader of about 1000 to 1040 and the great Hedeby ship of about 1025 (ship_classes_793.json later_types_not_in_table): unlock_ship_knarr and unlock_ship_hedeby_great_ship do nothing until then.

Counts the engine does not keep yet: kept commissions for one house (count:kept_commission x3), passages of one water (count:passages x3), sea crossings in a ship of your own (the three-crossings rule), hired pilots on one water.
A yearly render and a yearly keep taken at the winter reckoning (charters, factors, the Tiel and Sigtuna purses); a charter lapsing at an accession in its realm.
A reader aboard (Chest.ReaderAboard is a stub) and learned.runes below 1 as a fraction (the live game answers 0 or 1 for learned.latin only).
port.people and port.faith are in the grammar but the live game answers only port.kind, port.realm and port.id: conditions here use port.realm.
Ship upgrades: Data/story/ship_upgrades_793.json does not exist yet; the nine upgrade ids here can seed it.

The entries marked from_chain were found by scanning Data/encounters for 'flag unlock_...' when this file was built: chains written afterwards set flags that are not listed, and the kinds block still covers them by prefix.
The works here (unlock_work_...) and the stones among the memorials take their price, days and upkeep from story/works_793.json at build time: if that table is retuned, these numbers are stale.

Eight ship entries were added on 6 Oct 2026 so that every class of ship_classes_793.json has one (logboat, skiff_punt, west_small_boat, ferry_barge, raft, gaelic_wooden_ship, warship_west, norse_longship): the ferry and the levy ship are a right and a duty, not hulls to trade in, and their what_it_gives says so. They use flag.levy_served (winter_793.json) and act:audience; the ferry's yearly sums belong to the winter reckoning.
